title: The 'text/html' Media Type
summary: Summarizes the history of HTML development and defines the text/html media type by pointing to the relevant W3C recommendations. It is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC registers text/html as the media type for HTML documents and points to W3C Recommendations for the language definition. It also explains character encoding and other details needed to label and interpret HTML content.

subtitle: The registration of text/html and the handoff of HTML definition to the W3C.

tldr.problem: HTML had been described in multiple IETF documents, while the work of defining HTML had moved to the W3C.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers text/html, points to W3C Recommendations for the HTML definition, and describes parameters and encoding considerations.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes five earlier RFCs about HTML and removes HTML from the IETF Standards Track.

today: RFC 2854 is an Informational RFC published in June 2000. It obsoletes RFCs 1866, 1867, 1980, 1942, and 2070; the unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: How HTML Specification Work Changed
sections.content:
HTML was used on the World Wide Web from 1990 and was initially described in informal documents. The IETF HTML working group first defined the text/html media type in 1995 and produced documents for HTML and proposed extensions.

The IETF working group closed in September 1996, and work on defining HTML moved to the W3C. This RFC summarizes that history and obsoletes earlier IETF documents defining HTML.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF first documented HTML, then work on the language moved to the W3C. This memo records that change and retires the earlier IETF HTML documents.

sections.title: The text/html Media Type
sections.content:
The registration uses type text and subtype html. It has no required parameters. The optional charset parameter identifies the character encoding; any registered IANA charset may be used, and UTF-8 is preferred. The RFC strongly recommends including the parameter.

The HTML definition itself is in W3C Recommendations, with HTML 4.01 the latest version at the time. XHTML 1.0 may also be labeled text/html. The W3C has change control over the HTML specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The media type tells a recipient that the content is HTML. A charset parameter tells it how the document’s characters are encoded.

sections.title: Fragments, Line Breaks, and Character Sets
sections.content:
For text/html documents, a fragment identifier after the hash sign in a URI points to a named element. Elements can use the id attribute for this purpose, and some elements may also use name.

The MIME canonical form represents line breaks with a carriage return followed by a line feed. The RFC explains that MIME and HTTP had different default charset rules and recommends an explicit charset parameter to avoid ambiguity. HTTP also permits non-canonical line endings in some cases.
sections.plainLanguage: A fragment can point to a named part of an HTML document. An explicit character encoding helps different systems interpret the document’s text consistently.

sections.title: Recognizing HTML and Running Scripts
sections.content:
There is no single magic number that identifies every HTML file. The RFC says almost all HTML files have an <html string near the beginning, and many begin with a DOCTYPE declaration. File extensions such as html and htm are common but are not the formal media type.

HTML can contain scripts and interactive features. User agents that execute programs supplied by the sender must take care to run untrusted software in a protected environment.
sections.plainLanguage: No single opening marker identifies every HTML file, so file recognition may rely on its document structure. Browsers must isolate programs in pages because the sender may be untrusted.
